content.intro: In this lesson, you will study classification Metrics within Model Evaluation, Validation, and Reliability. You will connect the syllabus topics below to a small, inspectable example and practice stating what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Evaluation is part of system design, not an afterthought. A metric is useful only when it reflects the goal, data conditions, and error costs.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: A confusion matrix counts true and false predictions by class. Accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, F1, and curve-based metrics answer different questions, so choose based on error costs and class distribution.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus topics covered in this lesson

items.title: Confusion matrix
items.text: A confusion matrix counts correct and incorrect predictions by class. It shows error types that a single accuracy value can hide, especially for imbalanced classes.

items.title: Accuracy
items.text: Accuracy is the fraction of predictions that are correct. It can be misleading when one class dominates or errors have different consequences; compare with additional task-specific metrics.

items.title: Precision and recall
items.text: Precision measures how many predicted positives are correct; recall measures how many actual positives are found. Raising one can lower the other as the decision threshold changes.

items.title: Specificity
items.text: Specificity is one of the concepts used to reason about classification metrics. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

items.title: F1-score
items.text: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. It balances those two quantities but does not encode true negatives, probability calibration, or different real-world error costs.

items.title: ROC curves and AUC
items.text: An ROC curve summarizes true-positive versus false-positive rates across thresholds; AUC summarizes ranking performance over that curve. In highly imbalanced settings, precision–recall curves may better communicate positive-class behavior.

items.title: Precision–recall curves
items.text: Precision measures how many predicted positives are correct; recall measures how many actual positives are found. Raising one can lower the other as the decision threshold changes.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Identify what classification metrics takes as input and what result or decision it is intended to support. 2. Read the example before running it and predict the output. 3. Run the small example, compare actual and expected output, then change one input or assumption and repeat. 4. Record what the example demonstrates and what it does not demonstrate about a real system.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: Start with the task definition and the inputs available. Make the expected behavior explicit, choose a simple reference point, and inspect both ordinary examples and cases where assumptions may fail. Evaluation is part of system design, not an afterthought. A metric is useful only when it reflects the goal, data conditions, and error costs.

content_blocks.code:
true_positive, false_positive, false_negative = 8, 2, 4
precision = true_positive / (true_positive + false_positive)
recall = true_positive / (true_positive + false_negative)
print(f"precision: {precision:.2f}")
print(f"recall: {recall:.2f}")

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: If the output differs, check indentation and spelling, confirm you saved the intended file, and compare each input value with the example. If the example runs as expected, do not infer that it proves a trained model works; this snippet is a deterministic teaching aid. Keep sensitive data out of tests.

content_blocks.title: Check before you trust a result
content_blocks.text: This is a small, deterministic teaching example—not a trained AI model or evidence of production performance. Run it with a local Python 3 interpreter; do not paste secrets or private data into experiments.
